trap.wrong: "More code review and testing so mistakes don't happen."
trap.why: Mistakes will happen anyway. The question is about limiting blast radius and making undo fast.
trap.probe: Progressive delivery, cells, reversible changes, guardrails on destructive actions, tested recovery.
trap.say: "Assume mistakes: canary and progressive rollouts with automatic rollback, flags for instant off, cells to contain damage, deletion protection, and practised restores."

thesis: Assume mistakes will happen and design so each one has a small blast radius and a fast undo: progressive rollouts, reversible changes, feature flags, cells or shards that contain failures, backups with tested restores, and guardrails on destructive operations.
pitch: People will deploy bugs, push bad config, run the wrong command and delete the wrong thing. The goal is to make each of those cheap. I'd limit blast radius: progressive rollouts that start with a canary, one cell or one region and expand only if metrics stay healthy, with automatic rollback; cell-based architecture so a bad change or overload affects a fraction of customers. I'd make changes reversible: backward-compatible schema changes, feature flags that turn new behaviour off without a deploy, config changes versioned and quickly revertible. I'd add guardrails on destructive operations: soft delete, deletion protection on databases and buckets, confirmation and peer approval for dangerous commands, and least-privilege access so one mistake can't touch everything. And I'd make recovery real: tested backups and point-in-time restore. Culturally, blameless postmortems make people report and fix near-misses instead of hiding them.

points.d: Canary, then a small percentage, then wider, with automated health checks and rollback. Most bad changes are caught at a few percent of traffic.
Partition customers into independent cells; deploy and configure one cell at a time so failures stay contained.
Backward-compatible migrations, feature flags, and versioned config with one-step revert.
Deletion protection, soft delete, required approvals, dry-run modes, and rate limits on bulk operations.
Narrow permissions and separate production credentials so one mistake or compromised account can't affect everything.
Point-in-time recovery, backups in an isolated account, and regular restore drills.
Postmortems focus on how the system allowed the mistake, leading to better guardrails rather than blame.

decision: Invest first in fast rollback and progressive delivery (they catch the most common mistakes), then guardrails on destructive operations, then cell isolation as scale and risk grow.
numbers: Rollout example: 1% for 15 minutes, 10% for 30 minutes, 50% for 30 minutes, then 100%, with automatic rollback if error rate rises by more than a set threshold at any stage.
Cell math: with 20 cells, a bad change caught in the first cell affects about 5% of customers.
pitfalls: Global config pushes that apply everywhere at once.
Rollbacks that are possible in theory but never practised.
Production databases without deletion protection or point-in-time recovery.
Blame culture, so near-misses go unreported.

followups.q: How do you make config changes as safe as code deploys?
followups.a: Store config in version control, validate it in CI, roll it out progressively, and monitor and revert it like code.

followups.q: What's the most valuable guardrail to add first?
followups.a: Fast, practised rollback for deploys and config, because bad changes cause a large share of incidents.

followups.q: How do cells differ from shards?
followups.a: Cells are complete, independent copies of the service stack serving a subset of customers, so a failure or bad deploy in one doesn't spread; shards usually partition only the data.

example: A bad fee-calculation rule was deployed behind a flag to 2% of loans. Automated checks comparing fees with the previous version flagged anomalies within 10 minutes; the flag was turned off, 140 loans were corrected by a script, and no customer was charged incorrectly.
